items.title: From a vague idea to a system map: the workflow behind Zextha
items.summary: I’m building Zextha , a visual workspace for exploring the system around an idea. This is a short walkthrough of the product workflow and the decisions behind it. The problem: a prompt leaves things unsaid “I want to build a learning companion” describes an intention. It does not tell us who will use it, what environment it needs to work in, or how we will know it helps. Starting implementation immediately can hide those unknowns inside the design. Zextha gives the early thinking a visible structure: Describe the idea in your own words. Answer four questions tailored to that idea. Explore a map of perspectives and their relationships. Use the map to decide what to investigate or try next. Four questions should earn their place A fixed budget–goal–timeline checklist is convenient, but it can miss the questions that matter for a particular project. For a learning companion, device access and the learner’s context may be important. For a content creator, the audience and a sustainable format may matter more. These are examples of useful questions, not a promise that every generated session uses the same wording. The goal is to collect context that can change the map, while keeping the interaction short. A map is an interface for investigation A useful node should give you something to examine: a dependency, constraint, risk, choice, or next action. Connections help show why one decision affects another. For example, choosing an offline-first experience affects storage, synchronization, content updates, and how failures are explained. Treating “offline support” as a single checkbox would hide much of that work. The output still needs human review. A generated map is not an exhaustive architecture review or evidence that an idea will work. It is a way to make the next discussion more concrete. Reading and references have different jobs Zextha’s Notes area contains original field books with chapters that can be read inside the workspace. Documents helps readers understand why a reference matters and follow it to the original source. Keeping those experiences distinct matters: reading a chapter and evaluating a source are different tasks. An optional perspective for agents Zextha also exposes an MCP connection for compatible clients. An agent can request a read-only perspective on an idea, an approach, or next steps. It does not automatically inspect your files or take control of your project; the client supplies the context. The connection details are available in the MCP workspace . Try it with a real uncertainty If you explore Zextha , try an idea you are still unsure about. Look for one useful connection, then verify it against the real requirements. I’d welcome feedback from builders: what information would make a system map useful before you start implementation? Disclosure: I’m Zextha’s founder. This post was prepared with AI assistance.

I’m building Zextha, a visual workspace for exploring the system around an idea. This is a short walkthrough of the product workflow and the decisions behind it.

The problem: a prompt leaves things unsaid

“I want to build a learning companion” describes an intention. It does not tell us who will use it, what environment it needs to work in, or how we will know it helps. Starting implementation immediately can hide those unknowns inside the design.

Zextha gives the early thinking a visible structure:

  1. Describe the idea in your own words.
  2. Answer four questions tailored to that idea.
  3. Explore a map of perspectives and their relationships.
  4. Use the map to decide what to investigate or try next.
Four questions should earn their place

A fixed budget–goal–timeline checklist is convenient, but it can miss the questions that matter for a particular project.

For a learning companion, device access and the learner’s context may be important. For a content creator, the audience and a sustainable format may matter more. These are examples of useful questions, not a promise that every generated session uses the same wording.

The goal is to collect context that can change the map, while keeping the interaction short.

A map is an interface for investigation

A useful node should give you something to examine: a dependency, constraint, risk, choice, or next action. Connections help show why one decision affects another.

For example, choosing an offline-first experience affects storage, synchronization, content updates, and how failures are explained. Treating “offline support” as a single checkbox would hide much of that work.

The output still needs human review. A generated map is not an exhaustive architecture review or evidence that an idea will work. It is a way to make the next discussion more concrete.

Reading and references have different jobs

Zextha’s Notes area contains original field books with chapters that can be read inside the workspace. Documents helps readers understand why a reference matters and follow it to the original source.

Keeping those experiences distinct matters: reading a chapter and evaluating a source are different tasks.

An optional perspective for agents

Zextha also exposes an MCP connection for compatible clients. An agent can request a read-only perspective on an idea, an approach, or next steps. It does not automatically inspect your files or take control of your project; the client supplies the context.

The connection details are available in the MCP workspace.

Try it with a real uncertainty

If you explore Zextha, try an idea you are still unsure about. Look for one useful connection, then verify it against the real requirements.

I’d welcome feedback from builders: what information would make a system map useful before you start implementation?

Disclosure: I’m Zextha’s founder. This post was prepared with AI assistance.

items.title: Design a recommendation system: the ML system design interview walkthrough
items.summary: Design a recommendation system: the ML system design interview walkthrough The request to design a recommendation system sounds like one line — show users videos they will like — and that one line hides the whole interview. Do it for a tiny catalogue and you can score every item for every user; do it for a hundred million items with a 100-millisecond budget, learning from every click and surviving a brand-new user with no history, and it becomes a retrieval-plus-ranking-plus-data-pipeline problem with a dozen sharp edges. This is one of the most common recommendation system system design prompts because it is really a machine learning system design question in disguise: it forces every muscle at once — retrieval, embeddings, feature serving, training data, and the feedback loop. The round turns on one structural insight. "Show users videos they'll like" sounds like a single model, but you cannot score millions of candidate items per request inside a tight latency budget, so a real recommender is a two-stage pipeline — cheap candidate generation retrieves a few hundred items from the full catalogue, then an expensive ranking model scores just those few. Get that one reframe — it is retrieval then ranking, glued to an offline training pipeline by a feedback loop, not "pick an algorithm" — and the rest of the ML system design interview is deciding how to retrieve cheaply, how to rank well, and how logged interactions become tomorrow's training data. This walkthrough follows the path a strong candidate draws on the whiteboard — requirements, estimate, API and data model, high-level design, then the deep dives — and at each step it names the follow-up the interviewer uses to tell a memorised answer from an engineer who understands the tradeoff. How the recommendation system round is actually run A recommendation system round runs about 60 minutes on a shared canvas — you draw the boxes and arrows while you talk, and the interviewer interrupts. It is a favourite because the one-line problem opens onto deep water fast, and because it blends two things most candidates practise separately: the architecture reasoning of a high-level design round and the modelling reasoning of a machine learning round. The moment you draw "user asks, system returns a ranked list," the question becomes how do you avoid touching every item , and every answer after that — embeddings, features, training labels — compounds from the two-stage split. The interviewer rarely lets "score the items and sort them" stand. "The catalogue is a hundred million items and you have about a hundred milliseconds per request — how do you avoid scoring all of them?" That question — the latency-versus-coverage squeeze — is the one a copied answer can never rehearse, and the one this round is really testing. The rounds here are modelled on how the loop runs , not scraped from any candidate's recall. What matters for prep is the shape: a blank canvas, a clock, and a follow-up after every decision you make. The five-step framework for any HLD round Every high-level design answer fits the same spine. Say it out loud at the start so the interviewer knows you have a plan, then walk it: Clarify requirements — functional and non-functional, and what you are explicitly not building. Estimate — catalogue size, users, request rate and latency budget, and training-data volume, to justify every later choice. High-level design — the boxes and arrows: the serving path, candidate generation, ranking, and the offline training pipeline. Deep dive — the two or three decisions that actually decide this system. Follow-ups — bottlenecks, failure modes, and what you would change at ten times the scale. What the debrief measures The score is not "right or wrong design." items.summary_html:
Design a recommendation system: the ML system design interview walkthrough

The request to design a recommendation system sounds like one line — show users videos they will like — and that one line hides the whole interview. Do it for a tiny catalogue and you can score every item for every user; do it for a hundred million items with a 100-millisecond budget, learning from every click and surviving a brand-new user with no history, and it becomes a retrieval-plus-ranking-plus-data-pipeline problem with a dozen sharp edges. This is one of the most common recommendation system system design prompts because it is really a machine learning system design question in disguise: it forces every muscle at once — retrieval, embeddings, feature serving, training data, and the feedback loop.

The round turns on one structural insight. "Show users videos they'll like" sounds like a single model, but you cannot score millions of candidate items per request inside a tight latency budget, so a real recommender is a two-stage pipeline — cheap candidate generation retrieves a few hundred items from the full catalogue, then an expensive ranking model scores just those few. Get that one reframe — it is retrieval then ranking, glued to an offline training pipeline by a feedback loop, not "pick an algorithm" — and the rest of the ML system design interview is deciding how to retrieve cheaply, how to rank well, and how logged interactions become tomorrow's training data. This walkthrough follows the path a strong candidate draws on the whiteboard — requirements, estimate, API and data model, high-level design, then the deep dives — and at each step it names the follow-up the interviewer uses to tell a memorised answer from an engineer who understands the tradeoff.

How the recommendation system round is actually run

A recommendation system round runs about 60 minutes on a shared canvas — you draw the boxes and arrows while you talk, and the interviewer interrupts. It is a favourite because the one-line problem opens onto deep water fast, and because it blends two things most candidates practise separately: the architecture reasoning of a high-level design round and the modelling reasoning of a machine learning round. The moment you draw "user asks, system returns a ranked list," the question becomes how do you avoid touching every item, and every answer after that — embeddings, features, training labels — compounds from the two-stage split.

The interviewer rarely lets "score the items and sort them" stand. "The catalogue is a hundred million items and you have about a hundred milliseconds per request — how do you avoid scoring all of them?" That question — the latency-versus-coverage squeeze — is the one a copied answer can never rehearse, and the one this round is really testing.

The rounds here are modelled on how the loop runs, not scraped from any candidate's recall. What matters for prep is the shape: a blank canvas, a clock, and a follow-up after every decision you make.

The five-step framework for any HLD round

Every high-level design answer fits the same spine. Say it out loud at the start so the interviewer knows you have a plan, then walk it:

  1. Clarify requirements — functional and non-functional, and what you are explicitly not building.
  2. Estimate — catalogue size, users, request rate and latency budget, and training-data volume, to justify every later choice.
  3. High-level design — the boxes and arrows: the serving path, candidate generation, ranking, and the offline training pipeline.
  4. Deep dive — the two or three decisions that actually decide this system.
  5. Follow-ups — bottlenecks, failure modes, and what you would change at ten times the scale.
What the debrief measures

The score is not "right or wrong design." A good HLD debrief reads on four dimensions, and every move below maps to one: problem solving (did you reach a two-stage retrieve-then-rank pipeline with an offline training loop), communication (did you say why you cannot score the whole catalogue per request in one sentence), technical execution (embeddings and an ANN index, a feature store, logged outcomes as labels, A/B testing and cold start), and time management (did you spend your 60 minutes on candidate generation, ranking, and the feedback loop, not on which exact model architecture to use). Reading a walkthrough teaches the design; it does not teach you to deliver it on the clock while someone pushes back.

Step 1 — Requirements: what a recommendation system must do

Spend the first few minutes here. Jumping to boxes before you have scoped the problem is the fastest way to design the wrong system.

Type Requirement Functional Given a user and a context, return a personalised ranked list of items; serve several surfaces (home rows, "because you watched X", continue-watching, trending); refresh as the user interacts; return results fast enough to render inline. Functional (optional) Explicit controls (not-interested, thumbs), diversity and freshness rules, explanations for a row — call these out, then scope most of them for later. Non-functional Low latency per request (tens to ~100 ms); freshness (new items and new interactions reflected quickly); scale (hundreds of millions of users and items); measurable quality (offline metrics plus online engagement).

The sentence that earns points: "The hard part isn't choosing a model, it's serving a good ranked list in ~100 ms over a catalogue too large to score per request — so the core of the design is a two-stage retrieve-then-rank pipeline fed by an offline training loop, not a single model." Say that and you have framed the entire design before drawing a box.

Step 2 — Capacity estimation (back of the envelope)

Estimation here is about proving one thing: the hard axis is serving a good list cheaply at scale, which forces the two-stage split and the offline pipeline — not clever model choice.

Quantity Assumption Result Catalogue size millions to ~100M items you cannot score them all per request → retrieval must shrink the set first Users 100M+ active users precompute per-user candidates offline, or compute them online within budget Request rate + latency high QPS, ~100 ms budget cache candidates and features, retrieve with an ANN index — no full scan Training data billions of impression + interaction events/day a batch pipeline, not online scoring, builds the training set and the embeddings

Two conclusions fall out, and you should say both out loud. First, you must split retrieval from ranking — because the catalogue is too large to score per request, a cheap retrieval step narrows millions of items to a few hundred before any expensive model runs. Second, the heavy work lives offline: embeddings, candidate lists and model training run as batch jobs over logged events, and only the light retrieve-then-rank path runs online inside the latency budget. You have now pointed the interview at the real structure — two systems glued by logs — before anyone asked.

Step 3 — API and data model

The external API is deliberately small: one call returns a ranked list; the two internal stages sit behind it.

Operation Shape get_recommendations(user_id, context, k) the public call: given a user and a context (surface, time, device), return the top k ranked items. retrieve(user) -> candidates internal stage one: union several sources into a few hundred candidate items, cheaply. rank(user, candidates) -> ordered internal stage two: score the candidates with the ranking model and sort them.

The data model carries the state that both stages read and that the offline pipeline writes:

Entity Notes user profile plus a learned user embedding; the vector the retrieval and ranking stages key on. item the catalogue entry plus a learned item embedding and content features (genre, cast, length). interaction the log row — (user, item, action, timestamp) where action is impression / click / watch-time; the raw material for training labels. feature store precomputed batch features and freshly computed real-time features, keyed by user and item, read at ranking time.
Step 4 — High-level design: candidate generation plus ranking

Now the boxes. A client sends get_recommendations(user, context) to a recommendation service, which runs the two-stage path and returns a ranked list. Around that sit the pieces that make it fast and keep it learning:

  • Candidate generation (retrieval): unions several cheap sources — an approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) query over precomputed user/item embeddings, plus heuristic sources like trending, continue-watching and because-you-watched-X — into a few hundred candidates.
  • Ranking service: a heavier ML model scores those few hundred candidates using user, item and context features pulled from a feature store, then sorts them into the final list.
  • Feature store: serves batch features (precomputed offline) and real-time features (computed online) to the ranking model within the latency budget.
  • Logging stream: every impression and interaction is written to a stream — this is the raw data the offline side consumes.
  • Offline training pipeline: batch jobs turn logged events into training data, retrain the ranking model, and recompute embeddings and the ANN index; the resulting artefacts are pushed back to the serving path.
  • Experimentation layer: new models and retrieval sources ship behind A/B tests that measure real engagement, not just offline metrics.

Say explicitly that this is two systems glued by logs — an online, low-latency serving path (retrieve → rank) and an offline data-and-training path — and that the arrow from logged interactions back to training data is the feedback loop that makes it a recommender at all. Naming that unprompted is a signal the interviewer is listening for.

Deep dive: candidate generation and retrieval

This is the first decision that actually decides the round. The catalogue is too large to score per request, so where do the few hundred candidates come from, and why does that shape everything else?

The core move is to retrieve cheaply before you rank. The dominant source is collaborative filtering expressed as learned embeddings: a user and the items are mapped into the same vector space (often by a two-tower model — one tower for the user, one for items), and similar vectors mean "likely to be watched." At serving time you take the user's vector and ask an approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) index for the closest few hundred item vectors — approximate because an exact nearest-neighbour search over a hundred million vectors cannot fit the budget. Crucially, the embeddings and the ANN index are precomputed in a batch/offline job and refreshed periodically; the online step is just a fast vector lookup.

Retrieval source What it is for Embedding / ANN (collaborative filtering) the personalised core — ANN over learned user/item vectors surfaces items similar to what this user engages with. Trending / popularity a cheap, always-available source; strong for new or low-signal users and for freshness. Continue-watching / recent surfaces in-progress and recently viewed items directly from the user's own history. Because-you-watched-X (item-to-item) items whose embeddings are near a specific thing the user just watched; drives the "more like this" rows.

Real systems union several of these sources and dedupe, so no single retriever has to be perfect — breadth at stage one is cheap, and ranking sorts out the quality at stage two. Retrieval optimises recall (did the good items make the shortlist); precision is ranking's job.

"The catalogue is a hundred million items and you have a hundred milliseconds — how do you avoid scoring all of them?" You don't score them — you retrieve. Precompute user and item embeddings offline, build an ANN index, and at request time take the user's vector and fetch the nearest few hundred items, unioned with cheap sources like trending; only those few hundred reach the ranking model. The expensive model never sees the full catalogue.

System Design
HLD · Search & discovery · 60 min
Design a recommendation system out loud, with follow-ups

Practise on Zynter →

Deep dive: ranking, features and training data

This is the decision most candidates under-think. Retrieval hands you a few hundred candidates; the follow-up is always "how do you order them well, and where does the model's training signal even come from?"

Ranking is a heavier model on a small set. Because stage one already shrank millions of items to a few hundred, you can afford a richer model here — one that scores each candidate for this user, in this context, and sorts. The score is driven by three kinds of feature:

Feature type Examples User features long-term watch history and genres, embedding, demographics, device and session activity. Item features genre, cast, length, age, overall popularity, item embedding. Context features time of day, day of week, device, the surface being filled, what was just watched.

Those features come from a feature store: heavy, slow-changing features are precomputed in batch and cached, while real-time features (what the user did in the last few minutes) are computed online and merged in at request time — so the model sees fresh signal without recomputing everything per request.

The training label is the hard part, and it comes from the logs. You do not hand-label anything; you learn from logged impressions and their outcomes — did the user click, and how long did they watch. A common objective is expected watch time rather than raw clicks, because click-through alone rewards clickbait. Two biases must be named: position bias (items shown higher get more clicks regardless of quality) and the feedback bias that comes from only ever logging outcomes for items the system already chose to show — which is why the model can keep recommending what it already shows. You evaluate offline with ranking metrics like AUC or NDCG, but the decision to ship is made on online engagement from an A/B test, because offline wins do not always move real behaviour.

"Where does the training label come from, and why might the model keep recommending what it already shows?" The labels are logged outcomes — click and watch-time on the items you displayed — so the model only ever learns from items it already surfaced. That feedback bias, plus position bias, narrows what it shows over time; you counter it by logging impressions (not just clicks), adding exploration, and judging ships on online engagement, not offline AUC alone.

System Design
HLD · Search & discovery · 60 min
Defend ranking, features and training data out loud

Practise on Zynter →

Deep dive: the feedback loop, serving and cold start

Retrieval and ranking decide what to show; this decides whether the system stays fast and keeps learning. The follow-up is always the brand-new user.

Serving hits the budget by precomputing. The online path cannot afford to build everything per request, so candidates and features are precomputed and cached where possible: embeddings and the ANN index are built offline, batch features are refreshed on a schedule, and only the light retrieve-then-rank step with real-time features runs per request.

The feedback loop is the point. Every impression and interaction is logged to a stream, and that stream becomes tomorrow's training data: a batch pipeline turns raw events into labelled examples, the ranking model and embeddings are retrained periodically, and the fresh artefacts are pushed back to serving. That arrow — shown items → logged outcomes → new training data → better model → shown items — is the loop that makes the system a recommender rather than a static ranker.

Cold start is the case the interviewer reaches for. A model trained on history has nothing to go on when there is no history:

  • New user (no history): fall back to popularity and trending, use any onboarding signals (genres they picked, country, device), and lean on context; personalise as the first interactions arrive.
  • New item (no interactions): lean on content features (genre, cast, metadata, a content-based embedding) so it can be retrieved before it has engagement data; add light exploration so it gets shown enough to gather signal.

Ship behind A/B tests. New retrieval sources, features or models go out to a slice of traffic first, and the decision to roll out is made on real engagement, not on an offline metric that looked good — the same point the ranking deep dive made, now as a release discipline.

"A brand-new user signs up with zero history — what do you show, and how does the system start learning them?" You cannot personalise yet, so you fall back to trending and popularity, use onboarding signals and context, and keep the list diverse. The moment they interact, those impressions and outcomes are logged, flow into the training pipeline, and feed the next retrain — so the feedback loop bootstraps a personal model from the first few clicks.

The follow-ups that decide the recommendation system round

Scan the probes from each deep dive and they rhyme. Master these five and you are ready for a version of the question that is not drawn exactly like this one.

  • "Why two stages instead of one model?" → You cannot score a hundred million items per request in ~100 ms, so cheap retrieval shrinks the catalogue to a few hundred and an expensive ranker scores only those. (communication)
  • "How do you retrieve candidates without scanning the catalogue?" → Precompute user/item embeddings offline, build an ANN index, and fetch the nearest few hundred vectors at request time, unioned with trending and item-to-item sources. (problem solving)
  • "Where does the training label come from?" → Logged impressions and their outcomes — click and watch-time — not hand labels; you optimise something like expected watch time and watch for position and feedback bias. (technical execution)
  • "A brand-new user with no history — what do you show?" → Fall back to trending, popularity and onboarding signals, keep it diverse, and let the first logged interactions feed the retrain that personalises them. (problem solving)
  • "Your offline AUC went up — do you ship it?" → Not on that alone; ship behind an A/B test and decide on real engagement, because offline metrics do not always move online behaviour. (technical execution)

Each maps to a debrief dimension. Reading this list teaches you the answers; it does not teach you to deliver them while someone interrupts — that only comes from saying them out loud.

How to prepare: a one-week plan

You do not need fifty systems. You need this one cold and the framework automatic, so the next "design X" is just new nouns in the same five steps.

  • Days 1–2: Learn the five-step framework until it is reflex. Do the recommendation system end to end on paper — requirements, estimate, API, data model, the two-stage boxes plus the offline pipeline.
  • Days 3–4: Drill the retrieval deep dive: embeddings, the two-tower idea, ANN over precomputed vectors, and unioning cheap sources. Say in one sentence why you retrieve before you rank.
  • Days 5–6: Own ranking and the loop — user/item/context features from a feature store, labels from logged outcomes, position and feedback bias, offline-versus-online metrics, cold start, and A/B testing. Answer each of the five follow-ups out loud.
  • Day 7: A full timed 60-minute round, narrating the whole way, with someone (or something) interrupting. This is the rep that counts.

This post is the deep walkthrough behind one row of the broader Top 25 system design interview questions — once the recommendation system is automatic, the same spine carries the rest of the list.

Frequently asked questions How do I design a recommendation system step by step?

Follow the five-step HLD framework. Clarify requirements (a personalised ranked list across several surfaces, fast, fresh, measurable); estimate to show the catalogue is too large to score per request and that most work must run offline; define the small API (get_recommendations on the outside, retrieve and rank inside) with a user/item/interaction/feature-store model; draw the two-stage design (a recommendation service running candidate generation with an ANN over precomputed embeddings plus heuristic sources, then a ranking service backed by a feature store, with a logging stream feeding an offline training pipeline and an A/B layer); then deep-dive the decisions that matter — candidate generation, ranking and training data, and the feedback loop with cold start.

Why split a recommendation system into candidate generation and ranking?

Because you cannot score a huge catalogue for every request inside a tight latency budget. Candidate generation is a cheap retrieval step that shrinks millions of items to a few hundred — using an ANN query over precomputed embeddings plus sources like trending and item-to-item — optimising recall. Ranking is then an expensive model that scores only those few hundred with rich user, item and context features, optimising precision. The split lets you be both fast and accurate: broad and cheap first, precise and heavy second.

How does candidate generation use embeddings and ANN?

A model (often a two-tower model) maps users and items into the same vector space so that nearby vectors mean "likely to engage." Those embeddings are computed offline in a batch job and indexed in an approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) structure. At request time the system takes the user's vector and asks the ANN index for the closest few hundred item vectors — approximate because an exact search over a hundred million items would blow the latency budget — and unions that with cheap sources like trending and continue-watching. The online step is just a fast vector lookup, not a catalogue scan.

Where does the training data for the ranking model come from?

From the logs, not from hand labels. Every impression and its outcome — whether the user clicked and how long they watched — is logged to a stream and turned into labelled training examples by a batch pipeline. A common objective is expected watch time rather than raw clicks, so the model is not rewarded for clickbait. You must account for position bias (higher-placed items get more clicks) and feedback bias (you only see outcomes for items the system already showed), which is why real systems log impressions, add exploration, and judge ships on online engagement rather than offline metrics alone.

How do you handle cold start for a new user or new item?

For a brand-new user with no history you cannot personalise yet, so you fall back to popularity and trending, use any onboarding signals (chosen genres, country, device) and context, and keep the list diverse; the first logged interactions then flow into the training pipeline and bootstrap a personal model. For a new item with no interactions you lean on content features — genre, cast, metadata, a content-based embedding — so it can be retrieved before it has engagement data, plus a little exploration so it gets shown enough to gather signal.

How do I practise an ML system design interview out loud?

Reading a walkthrough is not the same as defending a design while someone interrupts. On Zynter, the HLD track runs live voice rounds modelled on how real system design loops run — you talk through a shared design on the canvas, and a voice interviewer pushes with the follow-ups above one at a time, then gives you a debrief on problem solving, communication, technical execution, and time management. The score is a practice signal, not a hiring decision.

Practise it on Zynter You can read every stage. The round is won on the two-stage split and the feedback loop.

Pick the Recommendation System round, draw the retrieve-then-rank pipeline and the offline training loop on the canvas, and defend it out loud to a voice interviewer that keeps asking "a hundred million items, a hundred milliseconds — how do you avoid scoring them all?" and "a brand-new user with zero history — what do you show?" — then read the debrief. items.title: MCP Explained for Frontend Developers: The USB-C of AI Integrations
items.summary: AI is everywhere today. We have GitHub Copilot writing code, ChatGPT answering questions, and AI agents capable of performing complex workflows. But there is one problem: every AI application needs a different way to connect with tools, databases, APIs, and services. Imagine buying a laptop that requires a different cable for charging, data transfer, and external displays. It would be frustrating. That's exactly how AI integrations have looked for a long time. Enter Model Context Protocol (MCP), a new standard designed to make AI systems communicate with external tools in a consistent way. In simple terms, MCP is like USB-C for AI applications. AI is everywhere today. We have GitHub Copilot writing code, ChatGPT answering questions, and AI agents capable of performing complex workflows. But there is one problem: every AI application needs a different way to connect with tools, databases, APIs, and services.

Imagine buying a laptop that requires a different cable for charging, data transfer, and external displays. It would be frustrating.

That's exactly how AI integrations have looked for a long time.

Enter Model Context Protocol (MCP), a new standard designed to make AI systems communicate with external tools in a consistent way.

In simple terms, MCP is like USB-C for AI applications.

The Problem Before MCP

Let's say you're building a frontend application that allows users to interact with an AI assistant.

Your AI needs to:

Read customer data
Fetch project details
Query a database
Create tickets in Jira
Access GitHub repositories

Without MCP, every integration requires custom implementation.

Frontend App
|
├── Custom GitHub API Integration
├── Custom Jira API Integration
├── Custom Database Connector
└── Custom Internal Service Connector

Every tool has:

Different authentication methods
Different request formats
Different response structures

As the number of tools grows, maintenance becomes difficult.

What is MCP?

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol that standardizes how AI models communicate with external systems.

Instead of building custom integrations for every tool, developers can expose functionality through an MCP server.

Frontend App
|
▼
AI Agent
|
▼
MCP Server
|
├── GitHub
├── Jira
├── Database
└── Internal APIs

The AI does not need to know how every system works internally.

It simply asks the MCP server for available tools and uses them when needed.

Why Should Frontend Developers Care?

Many frontend developers assume MCP is only for AI engineers.

That's not true.

If you're building:

AI-powered dashboards
Chat interfaces
Internal enterprise tools
Developer portals
Productivity applications

You'll likely interact with MCP-based systems sooner than you think.

For frontend developers, MCP offers three major benefits:

  1. Faster AI Integrations

You don't need to create separate integrations for every backend service.

The AI agent can discover available tools automatically.

  1. Cleaner Architecture

Instead of hardcoding API calls throughout the application, business actions can be exposed through MCP tools.

  1. Better Scalability

As new tools are added, the frontend often requires little or no changes.

The MCP server handles the complexity.

A Real-World Example

Imagine you're building a Project Management Assistant.

A user types:

Show all open bugs assigned to me and create a summary.

Without MCP:

Frontend calls Bug API
Frontend processes responses
Frontend calls AI API
Backend coordinates everything

With MCP:

User submits request
AI discovers available tools
AI calls Bug Tracker Tool
AI receives results
AI generates summary

The process becomes more intelligent and flexible.

MCP Components

There are three main components.

  1. MCP Host

The application where users interact with AI.

Examples:

AI chat applications
IDE extensions
Enterprise assistants

  1. MCP Client

Acts as the bridge between the host and the MCP server.

It sends requests and receives responses.

  1. MCP Server

Provides tools and resources that AI can use.

Examples:

GetUserDetails()
CreateJiraTicket()
FetchSalesReport()
SearchDocumentation()

The AI can discover and use these tools when needed.

Frontend Use Cases
Customer Support Portal

Users ask:

Show all unresolved support tickets from this week.

AI automatically retrieves data from connected systems.

Developer Dashboard

Users ask:

Show all failed deployments in production.

AI can fetch deployment logs through MCP tools.

Knowledge Management System

Users ask:

Summarize architecture documents related to authentication.

The AI retrieves documentation and generates insights.

A Simple Mental Model

Think of MCP as a restaurant.

User → Customer
AI → Waiter
MCP Server → Kitchen
Tools → Chefs

The customer doesn't walk into the kitchen.

The waiter knows which chef can prepare which dish.

Similarly, AI doesn't need direct knowledge of all systems.

It asks the MCP server for available tools and uses them when required.

Benefits of MCP
Reduced Development Effort

Build a tool once and expose it through MCP.

Multiple AI applications can reuse it.

Consistency

Every tool follows a common protocol.

Developers spend less time learning custom integrations.

Better User Experience

AI agents can accomplish tasks rather than just answer questions.

Future-Proof Architecture

As more organizations adopt AI agents, MCP provides a standardized integration layer.

Challenges to Consider

MCP is powerful, but it's not magic.

Security

Giving AI access to tools requires proper:

Authentication
Authorization
Audit logging
Tool Quality

Poorly designed tools lead to poor AI performance.

Monitoring

Track:

Tool usage
Failures
Response times

Just like any other API platform.

My Take

I believe MCP has the potential to become one of the most important standards in the AI ecosystem.

For frontend developers, the biggest shift is this:

We are moving from building applications that only display data to building applications that help users accomplish tasks through AI.

In the next few years, knowing how AI agents interact with tools may become just as important as understanding REST APIs or GraphQL today.

If you're a frontend developer exploring AI, now is a great time to learn MCP.

The earlier you understand it, the easier it will be to build the next generation of intelligent applications.

Final Thoughts

Frontend development has evolved from static pages to SPAs, then to cloud-connected applications, and now to AI-powered experiences.

MCP is another step in that evolution.

Instead of teaching AI about every system individually, we provide a standard way for systems to expose capabilities. The result is simpler integrations, smarter applications, and a better developer experience.

items.title: Build in public
items.summary: While building ShopPilot AI, I’ve been working on a function that checks availability for a requested product color and size. “Out of stock” and “that variant doesn’t exist” need different answers. I defined three cases to test: • The variant exists and has stock. • The variant exists but has zero stock. • There’s no matching variant. The interesting part was the third case. JavaScript’s .find() returns undefined when nothing matches, so I need to handle that before reading the variant’s stock. This is a small function, but it’s helping me connect JavaScript fundamentals, TypeScript, and testing to a real customer question. I’m learning how to use TDD for this logic: define the expected behavior with a failing test, implement it, then refactor. My main lesson so far: a useful test starts with a clear requirement. Before checking whether the code works, I need to decide what it should do.

items.summary: Prompt Improvement Techniques: A Practical Lesson Level: Beginner to Intermediate Estimated time: 30–45 minutes Goal: Learn how to write better prompts, improve AI responses iteratively, and use AI more effectively for coding, learning, research, and building projects. 1. The Fundamental Principle The biggest improvement you can make to your prompts is to stop asking AI for an answer and start specifying the outcome you want. Think of prompting like programming. A vague prompt is like passing incomplete arguments to a function. A clear prompt defines the inputs, constraints, and expected output. For example: Weak prompt: Teach me Ruby. Improved prompt: Act as an experienced Ruby engineer and mentor. I know basic Ruby, but I want to improve my debugging skills for entry-level software engineering interviews. Teach me through realistic examples, let me attempt solutions before showing the answers, and give me feedback on my reasoning. The second prompt defines the goal, context, teaching method, and expected interaction. Key principle: More words do not automatically produce better results. Relevant information matters more than length. 2. The Six Ingredients of a Strong Prompt 2.1 Goal What are you trying to accomplish? Weak: Make my app better. Better: Improve the onboarding experience so new users can complete their first workout log with less friction. 2.2 Context Give AI the information it needs to understand your situation. Example: This is an existing Ruby on Rails application. It already has authentication, workout models, and a dashboard. I want to improve the onboarding flow without rebuilding existing functionality. 2.3 Constraints Explain what AI should and should not do. Example: Preserve existing routes and database behavior. Avoid adding dependencies unless necessary. Do not refactor unrelated files. 2.4 Process Specify how AI should approach the task. Example: Inspect the current implementation, identify the root cause of the problem, propose the smallest reasonable change, and implement it only after explaining the approach. 2.5 Output Format Define what a useful response should contain. Example: Return the diagnosis, proposed fix, files affected, relevant tests, and any remaining risks. 2.6 Success Criteria Explain how you will judge whether the result is good. Example: The feature must work for authenticated users, handle invalid input, preserve existing behavior, and pass the relevant tests. You do not need all six ingredients in every prompt. Use the ones that materially affect the outcome. 3. The G-C-C-F Framework A simple framework for everyday prompting is: G — Goal: What outcome do you want? C — Context: What does AI need to know? C — Constraints: What rules must it follow? F — Format: What should the answer look like? Example: Learning Data Structures and Algorithms Goal: Prepare for entry-level software engineering interviews. Context: I know basic Ruby and have used Rails, but I need to strengthen my problem-solving skills. Constraints: Start with easy problems. Do not reveal solutions before I attempt them. Use idiomatic Ruby. Format: Give me one problem at a time, provide hints when needed, and evaluate correctness, efficiency, edge cases, and readability. Combined prompt: Act as an experienced Ruby engineer and interview coach. Help me prepare for entry-level software engineering interviews. I know basic Ruby and have used Rails, but I need to strengthen my data structures and algorithms skills. Start with easy problems and gradually increase the difficulty. Use idiomatic Ruby and do not reveal solutions before I attempt them. Give me one problem at a time, offer hints when needed, and evaluate correctness, efficiency, edge cases, and readability after each attempt. 4. The Ten Most Useful Iterative Prompting Techniques Iterative prompting means improving a response through successive, targeted instructions rather than expecting the first attempt to be perfect. Technique 1: Change One Thing at a Time If an answer is too long, do not rewrite the entire prompt. Instead, say: Keep the same content, but cut the length in half. Preserve the important examples and recommendations. This makes it easier to understand which adjustment improved the result. Technique 2: Diagnose Before Retrying Avoid repeatedly saying, "Try again." Instead, say: Identify the three biggest weaknesses in your previous answer. Explain what needs to change, then produce a revised version that addresses those weaknesses. This gives the next iteration a specific direction. Technique 3: Give Specific Feedback Weak feedback: I don't like it. Useful feedback: The explanation is accurate, but too theoretical. Use a practical Ruby example, explain what happens at each step, and finish with a short practice problem. Specific feedback is easier to act on than vague dissatisfaction. Technique 4: Define What Better Means Tell AI what criteria matter. Examples: Reduce the answer to 200 words. Improve readability without changing behavior. Include three realistic examples. Ensure the proposed solution handles empty input. Prioritize low-cost options with measurable benefits. For software, define success in terms of observable behavior and test results. Technique 5: Break Complex Tasks Into Stages For complicated work, use a sequence: Research the problem. Identify possible approaches. Compare trade-offs. Choose an approach. Implement the solution. Test the result. Review remaining risks. This gives you opportunities to catch misunderstandings before they become expensive mistakes. Technique 6: Request Alternatives When you do not know the best approach, ask AI to compare options. Give me three substantially different approaches. Explain their advantages, disadvantages, implementation costs, and risks. Recommend one based on my constraints. This is useful for architecture decisions, product features, career planning, and technical trade-offs. Technique 7: Ask Clarifying Questions When missing information could materially change the answer, tell AI to ask before proceeding. Identify the most important missing information. Ask me one clarifying question before making a recommendation. Do not use this unnecessarily for straightforward tasks. Clarification is most valuable when assumptions could lead to the wrong result. Technique 8: Verify Instead of Trusting Confidence A confident answer is not necessarily correct. For coding: Review the proposed solution against the requirements. Check edge cases, identify potential regressions, and run relevant tests if possible. Clearly distinguish verified results from assumptions. For research: Support important factual claims with reliable sources. Identify conflicting evidence and state when the available information is insufficient. Technique 9: Preserve What Already Works Prevent useful material from being rewritten unnecessarily. Keep sections one and two unchanged. Revise only section three to make it more practical. Preserve the original tone and examples. For code: Preserve existing behavior and unrelated functionality. Limit changes to the files necessary for the requested feature. Technique 10: Know When to Stop Do not continue revising indefinitely. Stop when the response meets your success criteria, important uncertainties have been addressed, and additional changes offer little value. Further revisions can introduce mistakes or waste time for marginal improvements. 5. Advanced Technique: Role Prompting Assigning AI a role can establish a useful perspective, but the role should be paired with specific responsibilities and evaluation criteria. Weak: Act as a senior developer. Better: Act as a senior Ruby engineer reviewing a junior developer's pull request. Prioritize correctness, readability, security, and maintainability. Identify serious issues first, explain why each matters, and avoid rewriting code that already works. The value comes from the expertise, priorities, and behavior you specify, not from the title alone. 6. Advanced Technique: Few-Shot Prompting Few-shot prompting means giving AI examples of the type of output you want. For example: Explain Ruby concepts using this format: Definition: One sentence. Simple example: A short code snippet. Real-world example: How the concept appears in an application. Common mistake: A typical error. Practice: One interview-style question. Examples establish a pattern that AI can follow consistently. Use this when you need structured lessons, consistent documentation, repeated code reviews, or standardized output across many tasks. 7. Advanced Technique: Prompt for a Process, Not Just an Answer For complicated tasks, explicitly define the sequence of work. Example: Help me add a workout history feature to an existing Rails application. Inspect the current models, routes, controllers, and views. Explain the existing architecture relevant to this feature. Propose a minimal implementation plan. Identify potential security and regression risks. Implement the feature in small, testable steps. Run relevant tests and report the actual results. Summarize changed files and remaining limitations. Preserve unrelated behavior and do not claim tests passed unless they were actually run. This is especially useful when working with AI coding agents that can inspect repositories, edit files, and execute commands. 8. Real-World Vibe Coding Techniques Vibe coding uses AI to accelerate software development. The most reliable workflow combines rapid generation with careful inspection and verification. Technique 1: Plan Before Generating Do not begin a large task by asking AI to build the entire application. Instead: Inspect my existing repository and explain how the relevant functionality works. Identify the files involved, propose the smallest safe implementation, and list potential risks. Do not modify any files yet. This prevents AI from inventing unnecessary architecture or replacing existing functionality. Technique 2: Make Changes in Small Slices For a workout logging feature, work incrementally: Display the form. Validate the input. Save the record. Display saved records. Add editing and deletion. Test permissions and edge cases. Each step should leave the application in a reasonably working state. Technique 3: Use the Smallest-Change Prompt Implement the requested feature with the smallest safe change. Preserve existing routes, APIs, styling conventions, database contracts, and behavior unless a change is necessary. Avoid unrelated refactoring and unnecessary dependencies. Explain the files changed and any potential regressions. This helps prevent scope creep. Technique 4: Provide Real Debugging Evidence When debugging, provide: Expected behavior. Actual behavior. Steps to reproduce the issue. Relevant error messages and logs. Recent changes. Relevant source code or test failures. Then ask: Trace the execution path and identify the most likely root cause based on the evidence. Explain your reasoning before proposing the smallest fix. Add a regression test that reproduces the original failure. Do not assume that the first visible error identifies the underlying cause. Technique 5: Generate Tests Alongside Features After implementing a feature, ask AI to: Identify critical success cases. Identify edge cases and failure modes. Write or update appropriate automated tests. Run the relevant tests if tool access permits. Report actual results and anything that could not be verified. Do not let AI weaken tests merely to make the implementation pass. Technique 6: Use Screenshots for Visual Iteration For interface work: Run the application. Capture the current interface. Provide a screenshot and describe the intended result. Ask AI to identify the most important visual differences. Fix one or two issues at a time. Capture another screenshot and compare. Screenshots help diagnose visual issues but do not establish that backend functionality works. Technique 7: Maintain a Project Brief Keep a short document containing: Application purpose and architecture. Important files and conventions. Requirements and decisions. Known bugs and technical debt. Tests last run and their results. The next concrete task. Ask AI to update the document after significant changes. This provides a reliable handoff between sessions. Technique 8: Use Git Checkpoints Before risky changes: Check the working tree with git status . Review existing changes. Commit or otherwise preserve a known-good state. Inspect the proposed changes. Run relevant tests. Prepare a rollback plan when data or production behavior is at risk. Do not blindly reset files or run destructive commands just because AI recommends them. 9. The Four-Stage Debugging and Refinement Loop When a feature does not work, avoid an endless sequence of "fix it" prompts. Use this process. Stage 1: Diagnose Trace the behavior from the user interface through the controller and model. Identify the likely root cause and the evidence supporting it. Do not edit files yet. Stage 2: Fix Implement the smallest fix for the identified root cause. Preserve unrelated behavior and explain which files changed. Stage 3: Verify Reproduce the original failure and run relevant tests. Report what actually passed, failed, or could not be run. Stage 4: Harden Identify likely edge cases that could still break the feature. Add regression tests and address any newly discovered issues. Each stage has a different purpose. Separating diagnosis, implementation, verification, and hardening makes failures easier to understand. 10. Common AI Coding Failure Modes Failure mode Better instruction Editing before understanding the app Inspect and explain the existing implementation first. Rewriting unrelated files Make the smallest safe change. Claiming tests passed without running them Report verified results separately from assumptions. Fixing symptoms repeatedly Trace the execution path and identify the root cause. Adding unnecessary dependencies Prefer existing dependencies unless there is a clear reason. Generating a huge feature in one pass Break implementation into small, testable steps. Ignoring regressions Compare the change against original requirements and existing tests. Overwriting important changes Review Git status and preserve a known-good state. 11. A Reusable Iterative Prompt Copy this template when you want AI to improve an existing answer or implementation. Let's improve your previous response iteratively. Evaluate it against my original goal. Identify the three most important weaknesses or gaps. Propose specific improvements instead of rewriting everything indiscriminately. Preserve the parts that already work. Produce a revised version that addresses the weaknesses. Explain briefly what changed and why. If important information is missing, ask me one clarifying question before revising. Do not invent facts or claim improvements that have not been verified. For code, add: Inspect the existing implementation before editing. Keep changes scoped to the requested outcome. Run relevant tests if possible and report the actual results, including failures and unverified assumptions. 12. Practice Exercise Challenge: Improve a Weak Coding Prompt Your goal is to add a workout history page to an existing Ruby on Rails application. Weak prompt: Add workout history to my app. Rewrite the prompt to include: The goal and relevant context. What AI should inspect before making changes. Constraints that preserve existing behavior. An incremental implementation strategy. Tests and success criteria. Example Answer Act as an experienced Ruby on Rails engineer working in an existing fitness application. Add a workout history page that allows authenticated users to view their previously saved workouts. Before editing, inspect the existing models, routes, controllers, views, authentication, and authorization rules. Explain the relevant architecture and propose the smallest safe implementation. Implement the feature in small steps, preserving existing behavior and styling conventions. Avoid unnecessary dependencies and unrelated refactoring. Ensure users can only access workouts they are authorized to view. Add appropriate tests for populated and empty histories, authentication, authorization, and relevant edge cases. Run the relevant tests if possible and report the actual results, files changed, and remaining limitations. Why This Prompt Is Better It defines the feature, gives the AI a discovery phase, limits unnecessary changes, establishes incremental implementation, addresses access control, and specifies how to verify success. 13. Final Rules of Thumb Inspect before editing. Give one primary goal per prompt. Provide context and real evidence. Make small, targeted changes. Diagnose before retrying. Preserve what already works. Verify results instead of trusting confidence. Use Git to protect working code. Understand the important parts of anything you ship. Stop iterating when the result meets your success criteria. The central lesson: Prompt engineering is specification writing, and iterative prompting is a feedback loop. The goal is not to make AI produce more output. It is to guide AI toward the right outcome, detect mistakes early, and improve results through evidence and targeted changes. For vibe coding specifically, the real skill is not merely generating code. It is making the right changes, understanding the important decisions, catching incorrect assumptions, and shipping reliable software faster.

  • Reduce the answer to 200 words.
  • Improve readability without changing behavior.
  • Include three realistic examples.
  • Ensure the proposed solution handles empty input.
  • Prioritize low-cost options with measurable benefits.

For software, define success in terms of observable behavior and test results.

Technique 5: Break Complex Tasks Into Stages

For complicated work, use a sequence:

  1. Research the problem.
  2. Identify possible approaches.
  3. Compare trade-offs.
  4. Choose an approach.
  5. Implement the solution.
  6. Test the result.
  7. Review remaining risks.

This gives you opportunities to catch misunderstandings before they become expensive mistakes.

Technique 6: Request Alternatives

When you do not know the best approach, ask AI to compare options.

Give me three substantially different approaches. Explain their advantages, disadvantages, implementation costs, and risks. Recommend one based on my constraints.

This is useful for architecture decisions, product features, career planning, and technical trade-offs.

Technique 7: Ask Clarifying Questions

When missing information could materially change the answer, tell AI to ask before proceeding.

Identify the most important missing information. Ask me one clarifying question before making a recommendation.

Do not use this unnecessarily for straightforward tasks. Clarification is most valuable when assumptions could lead to the wrong result.

Technique 8: Verify Instead of Trusting Confidence

A confident answer is not necessarily correct.

For coding:

Review the proposed solution against the requirements. Check edge cases, identify potential regressions, and run relevant tests if possible. Clearly distinguish verified results from assumptions.

For research:

Support important factual claims with reliable sources. Identify conflicting evidence and state when the available information is insufficient.

Technique 9: Preserve What Already Works

Prevent useful material from being rewritten unnecessarily.

Keep sections one and two unchanged. Revise only section three to make it more practical. Preserve the original tone and examples.

For code:

Preserve existing behavior and unrelated functionality. Limit changes to the files necessary for the requested feature.

Technique 10: Know When to Stop

Do not continue revising indefinitely.

Stop when the response meets your success criteria, important uncertainties have been addressed, and additional changes offer little value.

Further revisions can introduce mistakes or waste time for marginal improvements.

5. Advanced Technique: Role Prompting

Assigning AI a role can establish a useful perspective, but the role should be paired with specific responsibilities and evaluation criteria.

Weak:

Act as a senior developer.

Better:

Act as a senior Ruby engineer reviewing a junior developer's pull request. Prioritize correctness, readability, security, and maintainability. Identify serious issues first, explain why each matters, and avoid rewriting code that already works.

The value comes from the expertise, priorities, and behavior you specify, not from the title alone.

6. Advanced Technique: Few-Shot Prompting

Few-shot prompting means giving AI examples of the type of output you want.

For example:

Explain Ruby concepts using this format:

Definition: One sentence.

Simple example: A short code snippet.

Real-world example: How the concept appears in an application.

Common mistake: A typical error.

Practice: One interview-style question.

Examples establish a pattern that AI can follow consistently.

Use this when you need structured lessons, consistent documentation, repeated code reviews, or standardized output across many tasks.

7. Advanced Technique: Prompt for a Process, Not Just an Answer

For complicated tasks, explicitly define the sequence of work.

Example:

Help me add a workout history feature to an existing Rails application.

  1. Inspect the current models, routes, controllers, and views.
  2. Explain the existing architecture relevant to this feature.
  3. Propose a minimal implementation plan.
  4. Identify potential security and regression risks.
  5. Implement the feature in small, testable steps.
  6. Run relevant tests and report the actual results.
  7. Summarize changed files and remaining limitations.

Preserve unrelated behavior and do not claim tests passed unless they were actually run.

This is especially useful when working with AI coding agents that can inspect repositories, edit files, and execute commands.

8. Real-World Vibe Coding Techniques

Vibe coding uses AI to accelerate software development. The most reliable workflow combines rapid generation with careful inspection and verification.

Technique 1: Plan Before Generating

Do not begin a large task by asking AI to build the entire application.

Instead:

Inspect my existing repository and explain how the relevant functionality works. Identify the files involved, propose the smallest safe implementation, and list potential risks. Do not modify any files yet.

This prevents AI from inventing unnecessary architecture or replacing existing functionality.

Technique 2: Make Changes in Small Slices

For a workout logging feature, work incrementally:

  1. Display the form.
  2. Validate the input.
  3. Save the record.
  4. Display saved records.
  5. Add editing and deletion.
  6. Test permissions and edge cases.

Each step should leave the application in a reasonably working state.

Technique 3: Use the Smallest-Change Prompt

Implement the requested feature with the smallest safe change. Preserve existing routes, APIs, styling conventions, database contracts, and behavior unless a change is necessary. Avoid unrelated refactoring and unnecessary dependencies. Explain the files changed and any potential regressions.

This helps prevent scope creep.

Technique 4: Provide Real Debugging Evidence

When debugging, provide:

  • Expected behavior.
  • Actual behavior.
  • Steps to reproduce the issue.
  • Relevant error messages and logs.
  • Recent changes.
  • Relevant source code or test failures.

Then ask:

Trace the execution path and identify the most likely root cause based on the evidence. Explain your reasoning before proposing the smallest fix. Add a regression test that reproduces the original failure.

Do not assume that the first visible error identifies the underlying cause.

Technique 5: Generate Tests Alongside Features

After implementing a feature, ask AI to:

  1. Identify critical success cases.
  2. Identify edge cases and failure modes.
  3. Write or update appropriate automated tests.
  4. Run the relevant tests if tool access permits.
  5. Report actual results and anything that could not be verified.

Do not let AI weaken tests merely to make the implementation pass.

Technique 6: Use Screenshots for Visual Iteration

For interface work:

  1. Run the application.
  2. Capture the current interface.
  3. Provide a screenshot and describe the intended result.
  4. Ask AI to identify the most important visual differences.
  5. Fix one or two issues at a time.
  6. Capture another screenshot and compare.

Screenshots help diagnose visual issues but do not establish that backend functionality works.

Technique 7: Maintain a Project Brief

Keep a short document containing:

  • Application purpose and architecture.
  • Important files and conventions.
  • Requirements and decisions.
  • Known bugs and technical debt.
  • Tests last run and their results.
  • The next concrete task.

Ask AI to update the document after significant changes. This provides a reliable handoff between sessions.

Technique 8: Use Git Checkpoints

Before risky changes:

  1. Check the working tree with git status.
  2. Review existing changes.
  3. Commit or otherwise preserve a known-good state.
  4. Inspect the proposed changes.
  5. Run relevant tests.
  6. Prepare a rollback plan when data or production behavior is at risk.

Do not blindly reset files or run destructive commands just because AI recommends them.

9. The Four-Stage Debugging and Refinement Loop

When a feature does not work, avoid an endless sequence of "fix it" prompts.

Use this process.

Stage 1: Diagnose

Trace the behavior from the user interface through the controller and model. Identify the likely root cause and the evidence supporting it. Do not edit files yet.

Stage 2: Fix

Implement the smallest fix for the identified root cause. Preserve unrelated behavior and explain which files changed.

Stage 3: Verify

Reproduce the original failure and run relevant tests. Report what actually passed, failed, or could not be run.

Stage 4: Harden

Identify likely edge cases that could still break the feature. Add regression tests and address any newly discovered issues.

Each stage has a different purpose. Separating diagnosis, implementation, verification, and hardening makes failures easier to understand.

10. Common AI Coding Failure Modes
Failure mode Better instruction Editing before understanding the app Inspect and explain the existing implementation first. Rewriting unrelated files Make the smallest safe change. Claiming tests passed without running them Report verified results separately from assumptions. Fixing symptoms repeatedly Trace the execution path and identify the root cause. Adding unnecessary dependencies Prefer existing dependencies unless there is a clear reason. Generating a huge feature in one pass Break implementation into small, testable steps. Ignoring regressions Compare the change against original requirements and existing tests. Overwriting important changes Review Git status and preserve a known-good state.
11. A Reusable Iterative Prompt

Copy this template when you want AI to improve an existing answer or implementation.

Let's improve your previous response iteratively.

  1. Evaluate it against my original goal.
  2. Identify the three most important weaknesses or gaps.
  3. Propose specific improvements instead of rewriting everything indiscriminately.
  4. Preserve the parts that already work.
  5. Produce a revised version that addresses the weaknesses.
  6. Explain briefly what changed and why.

If important information is missing, ask me one clarifying question before revising. Do not invent facts or claim improvements that have not been verified.

For code, add:

Inspect the existing implementation before editing. Keep changes scoped to the requested outcome. Run relevant tests if possible and report the actual results, including failures and unverified assumptions.

12. Practice Exercise Challenge: Improve a Weak Coding Prompt

Your goal is to add a workout history page to an existing Ruby on Rails application.

Weak prompt:

Add workout history to my app.

Rewrite the prompt to include:

  • The goal and relevant context.
  • What AI should inspect before making changes.
  • Constraints that preserve existing behavior.
  • An incremental implementation strategy.
  • Tests and success criteria.
Example Answer

Act as an experienced Ruby on Rails engineer working in an existing fitness application. Add a workout history page that allows authenticated users to view their previously saved workouts.

Before editing, inspect the existing models, routes, controllers, views, authentication, and authorization rules. Explain the relevant architecture and propose the smallest safe implementation.

Implement the feature in small steps, preserving existing behavior and styling conventions. Avoid unnecessary dependencies and unrelated refactoring. Ensure users can only access workouts they are authorized to view.

Add appropriate tests for populated and empty histories, authentication, authorization, and relevant edge cases. Run the relevant tests if possible and report the actual results, files changed, and remaining limitations.

Why This Prompt Is Better

It defines the feature, gives the AI a discovery phase, limits unnecessary changes, establishes incremental implementation, addresses access control, and specifies how to verify success.

13. Final Rules of Thumb
  1. Inspect before editing.
  2. Give one primary goal per prompt.
  3. Provide context and real evidence.
  4. Make small, targeted changes.
  5. Diagnose before retrying.
  6. Preserve what already works.
  7. Verify results instead of trusting confidence.
  8. Use Git to protect working code.
  9. Understand the important parts of anything you ship.
  10. Stop iterating when the result meets your success criteria.

The central lesson: Prompt engineering is specification writing, and iterative prompting is a feedback loop. The goal is not to make AI produce more output. It is to guide AI toward the right outcome, detect mistakes early, and improve results through evidence and targeted changes.

For vibe coding specifically, the real skill is not merely generating code. It is making the right changes, understanding the important decisions, catching incorrect assumptions, and shipping reliable software faster.
