items.title: maestro 1.4.0 adds custom pipeline metrics
items.summary_html:
[This article was first published on data-in-flight, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

The 1.4.0 release of maestro is out, and with it comes the ability to record custom metrics from your pipelines. Execution time and success/failure were already tracked, but there was no good way to answer questions like “how many rows did this pipeline process?” or “how many API calls did it take?” Now there is.

If you haven’t heard of maestro, it’s a pipeline orchestration package. You can learn more about it here.

Get it from CRAN:

install.packages("maestro")
Recording metrics with update_metric()

A metric is any value that can be represented as a single number: rows processed, bytes read, API calls made, attempts on a task. To record one, call update_metric() from inside a pipeline with the name of the metric and its value. maestro automatically attributes the metric to the pipeline (and run) that is currently executing.

An important design point is that metrics are recorded on the side. They are not part of a pipeline’s return value, so they never get passed downstream in a DAG.

Here’s a two-step DAG that extracts some flight data and loads it, recording a few metrics along the way:

#' ./pipelines/metric_example.R
#' @maestroFrequency 1 hour
extract_flights <- function() {
  
  # Pretends to fetch data from an API
  df <- data.frame(
    flight_id = 1:5,
    airline_code = c("UA", "AC", "AC", "AA", "DE"),
    departure_time = as.POSIXct("2026-10-14 12:00:00") + c(100, 450, 750, 1450, 1750)
  )
  
  update_metric("rows_read", nrow(df))
  update_metric("bytes_read", as.numeric(object.size(df)))
  
  df
}

#' @maestroInputs extract_flights
load_flights <- function(.input) {
  
  write.csv(.input, tempfile(fileext = ".csv"))
  
  update_metric("rows_written", nrow(.input))
}
Retrieving metrics with get_metrics()

After running the schedule, get_metrics() returns a long data.frame of every metric recorded. Each row gives the pipeline it came from (pipe_name), the run it was recorded in (run_id), the metric name, and its numeric value.

library(maestro)

schedule <- build_schedule(quiet = TRUE)

status <- run_schedule(
  schedule,
  orch_frequency = "1 hour",
  quiet = TRUE
)

get_metrics(schedule)
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  pipe_name       run_id metric       value
                       
1 extract_flights vPnJoC rows_read        5
2 extract_flights vPnJoC bytes_read    1648
3 load_flights    ulLl5m rows_written     5

Notice that each pipeline gets its own run_id, even within a DAG. Because the result is a plain data.frame, it’s easy to summarise further or write out to a database or file, which makes it a natural fit for monitoring pipeline health over time.

A couple of other things to know:

  • Metrics are only recorded when a pipeline is executed by run_schedule(). Calling update_metric() while developing or testing a pipeline function interactively is harmless: it emits an informational message and does nothing.
  • Execution time and success/failure are already available via get_status() and get_schedule(), so there’s no need to record those yourself.
Metrics are per execution

Metrics belong to a single execution of a pipeline. Each time a pipeline runs it gets a new run_id, and its metrics are stored separately from those of earlier runs. Within one execution, calling update_metric() again with the same name overwrites the earlier value (the last write wins).

Running the schedule a second time shows this: the metrics from both runs are retained and distinguished by run_id.

status <- run_schedule(
  schedule,
  orch_frequency = "1 hour",
  quiet = TRUE
)

get_metrics(schedule)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  pipe_name       run_id metric       value
                       
1 extract_flights vPnJoC rows_read        5
2 extract_flights vPnJoC bytes_read    1648
3 extract_flights bilN7s rows_read        5
4 extract_flights bilN7s bytes_read    1648
5 load_flights    ulLl5m rows_written     5
6 load_flights    R9iMP0 rows_written     5
Accumulating with increment = TRUE

Sometimes a metric is built up over the course of a pipeline rather than computed once, like counting API calls inside a loop or the number of attempts on a flaky task. Setting increment = TRUE adds value to the metric’s current value instead of overwriting it. If the metric hasn’t been set yet in the current run, the first call simply sets it. A negative value decrements.

#' ./pipelines/metric_increment.R
#' @maestroFrequency 1 day
fetch_paginated <- function() {
  
  results <- list()
  
  for (page in 1:3) {
    attempts <- 0
    
    repeat {
      attempts <- attempts + 1
      update_metric("attempts", 1, increment = TRUE)
      
      # Pretends to call an API that sometimes fails
      ok <- runif(1) > 0.5
      if (ok || attempts >= 3) break
    }
    
    update_metric("api_calls", 1, increment = TRUE)
    results[[page]] <- data.frame(page = page, value = rnorm(10))
  }
  
  df <- do.call(rbind, results)
  
  # Overwriting (the default) is fine for a one-off value
  update_metric("rows_read", nrow(df))
  
  df
}

In this example both api_calls and attempts accumulate. When it finishes, api_calls is 3 (one per page) while attempts is at least 3, depending on how many retries were needed. Each metric still ends up with a single value per pipeline run.

For the full details, see the metrics vignette.

Other recent changes

If you missed the 1.3.x releases, there are a couple of smaller things worth mentioning:

  • The new @maestroCascadeTags tag propagates selected metadata tags (label, flags, and/or loglevel) from a pipeline to all of its downstream pipelines in a DAG. With no value, it cascades all three.
  • get_slot_usage() gained min_datetime and max_datetime parameters so the time window can be fixed rather than anchored to the current time.

The full list of changes is in the release notes.

As always, happy orchestrating!

items.title: The Human Advantage: Where AI Feedback Falls Short in Speaking Practice
items.summary: Artificial intelligence has changed speaking practice rather quickly. Now, learners can rehearse presentations and test pronunciation. They can also simulate interviews and receive instant corrections. They do not have to arrange a session with another person. Of course, it is convenient and sometimes remarkably useful. Still, speaking is a lot more than producing grammatically acceptable sentences. Meanwhile, human conversation remains unpredictable, emotionally charged, and deeply contextual. For instance, a speaker may choose the correct words. Still, they might sound hesitant, dismissive, rehearsed, or strangely detached. AI feedback can identify language patterns. However, human feedback often explains what those patterns actually mean inside a living conversation. That distinction matters more than it first appears. 1. Context Changes the Meaning of Good Speech Experienced teachers understand that effective speaking depends on – The situation Relationship Cultural setting Purpose of the exchange. For instance, iTalki tutors can notice when a learner sounds technically accurate but socially awkward. Then, they might suggest language that feels warmer, more natural, or more appropriate for a particular audience. That kind of adjustment comes from human judgment. It is obviously not mere error detection. Meanwhile, AI tools generally evaluate speech against recognisable linguistic patterns. They may flag – Filler words Repetition Pronunciation problems Unclear sentence structures. Still, they can struggle when a speaker deliberately breaks a rule for humour, emphasis, diplomacy, or personal style . Usually, human listeners recognise that intention faster. More importantly, they will explain whether it worked. 2. Emotional Nuance Requires Human Interpretation Speaking practice can expose insecurity. For instance, a learner may – Lower their voice after making a mistake Avoid difficult expressions Rush through an answer to prevent interruption. Although AI can measure pace and volume, it may not understand why those changes occurred. Meanwhile, a human coach can connect the behaviour to – Anxiety Uncertainty Fear of judgment. As a result, the feedback becomes more precise. Instead of saying, “Speak more slowly,” a teacher might explain that the learner accelerates when discussing unfamiliar subjects. That observation identifies a trigger rather than treating the symptom. It also gives the learner something practical to watch during future conversations. Human feedback also carries emotional weight. It might be a well-timed nod, a short pause, or a calm correction. These can reassure a learner without lowering expectations. By contrast, constant automated scoring may turn speaking into a performance dashboard. Useful for tracking, perhaps. Not always useful for confidence. 3. Human and AI Feedback Solve Different Problems The strongest distinction becomes clearer when both feedback types sit side by side. AI performs well when the task involves consistency, repetition, and measurable language features. Humans become more valuable when meaning depends on interpretation, personality, or changing social conditions. Area of Speaking Practice AI Feedback Human Feedback Pronunciation patterns Detects recurring sound errors quickly Explains which errors affect real-world understanding Grammar and vocabulary Identifies common mistakes consistently Distinguishes mistakes from intentional stylistic choices Tone and emotional impact Measures pitch, pace, and volume Interprets warmth, confidence, discomfort, and credibility Cultural suitability Offers general language conventions Adapts guidance to specific relationships and settings Conversation management Simulates predictable exchanges Responds naturally to hesitation, humour, tension, and interruption Therefore, treating human and AI feedback as direct substitutes misses the larger point. They operate at different levels. AI often describes visible features of speech, while a skilled person interprets the social effect those features produce. 4. Unscripted Interaction Exposes Hidden Weaknesses Many learners speak comfortably when answering familiar prompts. However, real conversations rarely follow clean scripts. People interrupt, change topics, misunderstand references, or respond with unexpected emotion. Human practice introduces this messiness naturally, and that is precisely why it remains valuable. During live interaction, a teacher can test whether the learner can: Clarify a misunderstood point without becoming defensive. Adjust an explanation after noticing confusion. Re-enter a conversation after interruption or hesitation. These abilities are difficult to reduce to a score. Moreover, they depend on awareness of another person’s reactions. AI simulations can imitate disruption, but they usually operate within designed boundaries. Human responses remain less predictable, and therefore closer to the conditions learners eventually face. 5. Fluency Alone Cannot Judge Credibility In most cases, professional speaking requires credibility rather than perfect fluency. For instance, the following issues must sound trustworthy: The manager presenting difficult news A candidate answering an interview question A specialist explaining a technical issue. Of course, grammar matters. Nevertheless, audiences also judge – Restraint Confidence Timing Sincerity. Human reviewers can detect when polished language begins to sound memorised. They may notice that an answer contains strong vocabulary but avoids the actual question. Likewise, they can identify when excessive formality creates distance. AI may praise structural accuracy in the same response because the measurable components remain sound. Furthermore, human feedback can challenge the speaker’s reasoning. A coach may ask whether an argument feels convincing, whether an example supports the claim, or whether the speaker has considered another interpretation. At that point, speaking practice becomes thinking practice too. The value moves well beyond pronunciation. 6. Personalised Feedback Needs Memory and Judgment AI systems can store progress data and adapt exercises to previous performance. Even so, meaningful personalisation requires more than remembering errors. A human teacher can recognise that a learner communicates confidently about work but becomes guarded during informal conversation. That pattern may reflect – Personality Experience Cultural habit. Accordingly, the teacher can decide when to correct or when to challenge. They can then judge when to let the conversation continue. Immediate correction sometimes helps. At other times, it destroys momentum. Human instructors make that judgment in real time. They use subtle signals that automated systems may overlook or misread. Better Speaking Emerges From a Hybrid Model AI feedback works best as a practice multiplier. It offers repetition, availability, and fast detection of surface-level problems. Human feedback provides interpretation, adaptation, emotional awareness, and social realism. Neither contribution needs exaggeration. For routine drills, automated tools can save time. They reveal patterns that learners might otherwise miss. However, human feedback still holds the stronger position when the goal involves – Persuasion Cultural sensitivity Spontaneity Trust Genuine conversational confidence. The practical model is hybrid. Use AI to practise frequently and track recurring issues. Then use human sessions to test whether improved speech actually lands well with another person. Because in the end, successful speaking is not simply speech that a system can analyse. It is speech that another human being can understand, trust, and respond to.

Artificial intelligence has changed speaking practice rather quickly. Now, learners can rehearse presentations and test pronunciation. They can also simulate interviews and receive instant corrections. They do not have to arrange a session with another person.

Of course, it is convenient and sometimes remarkably useful. Still, speaking is a lot more than producing grammatically acceptable sentences.

Meanwhile, human conversation remains unpredictable, emotionally charged, and deeply contextual. For instance, a speaker may choose the correct words. Still, they might sound hesitant, dismissive, rehearsed, or strangely detached.

AI feedback can identify language patterns. However, human feedback often explains what those patterns actually mean inside a living conversation. That distinction matters more than it first appears.

1. Context Changes the Meaning of Good Speech

Experienced teachers understand that effective speaking depends on –

  1. The situation
  2. Relationship
  3. Cultural setting
  4. Purpose of the exchange.

For instance, iTalki tutors can notice when a learner sounds technically accurate but socially awkward. Then, they might suggest language that feels warmer, more natural, or more appropriate for a particular audience.

That kind of adjustment comes from human judgment. It is obviously not mere error detection.

Meanwhile, AI tools generally evaluate speech against recognisable linguistic patterns. They may flag –

  • Filler words
  • Repetition
  • Pronunciation problems
  • Unclear sentence structures.

Still, they can struggle when a speaker deliberately breaks a rule for humour, emphasis, diplomacy, or personal style. Usually, human listeners recognise that intention faster. More importantly, they will explain whether it worked.

2. Emotional Nuance Requires Human Interpretation

Speaking practice can expose insecurity. For instance, a learner may –

  • Lower their voice after making a mistake
  • Avoid difficult expressions
  • Rush through an answer to prevent interruption.

Although AI can measure pace and volume, it may not understand why those changes occurred. Meanwhile, a human coach can connect the behaviour to –

  1. Anxiety
  2. Uncertainty
  3. Fear of judgment.

As a result, the feedback becomes more precise. Instead of saying, “Speak more slowly,” a teacher might explain that the learner accelerates when discussing unfamiliar subjects. That observation identifies a trigger rather than treating the symptom. It also gives the learner something practical to watch during future conversations.

Human feedback also carries emotional weight. It might be a well-timed nod, a short pause, or a calm correction. These can reassure a learner without lowering expectations.

By contrast, constant automated scoring may turn speaking into a performance dashboard. Useful for tracking, perhaps. Not always useful for confidence.

3. Human and AI Feedback Solve Different Problems

The strongest distinction becomes clearer when both feedback types sit side by side. AI performs well when the task involves consistency, repetition, and measurable language features.

Humans become more valuable when meaning depends on interpretation, personality, or changing social conditions.

Area of Speaking PracticeAI FeedbackHuman FeedbackPronunciation patternsDetects recurring sound errors quicklyExplains which errors affect real-world understandingGrammar and vocabularyIdentifies common mistakes consistentlyDistinguishes mistakes from intentional stylistic choicesTone and emotional impactMeasures pitch, pace, and volumeInterprets warmth, confidence, discomfort, and credibilityCultural suitabilityOffers general language conventionsAdapts guidance to specific relationships and settingsConversation managementSimulates predictable exchangesResponds naturally to hesitation, humour, tension, and interruption

Therefore, treating human and AI feedback as direct substitutes misses the larger point. They operate at different levels. AI often describes visible features of speech, while a skilled person interprets the social effect those features produce.

4. Unscripted Interaction Exposes Hidden Weaknesses

Many learners speak comfortably when answering familiar prompts. However, real conversations rarely follow clean scripts.

People interrupt, change topics, misunderstand references, or respond with unexpected emotion. Human practice introduces this messiness naturally, and that is precisely why it remains valuable.

During live interaction, a teacher can test whether the learner can:

  • Clarify a misunderstood point without becoming defensive.
  • Adjust an explanation after noticing confusion.
  • Re-enter a conversation after interruption or hesitation.

These abilities are difficult to reduce to a score. Moreover, they depend on awareness of another person’s reactions.

AI simulations can imitate disruption, but they usually operate within designed boundaries. Human responses remain less predictable, and therefore closer to the conditions learners eventually face.

5. Fluency Alone Cannot Judge Credibility

In most cases, professional speaking requires credibility rather than perfect fluency. For instance, the following issues must sound trustworthy:

  • The manager presenting difficult news
  • A candidate answering an interview question
  • A specialist explaining a technical issue.

Of course, grammar matters. Nevertheless, audiences also judge –

  1. Restraint
  2. Confidence
  3. Timing
  4. Sincerity.

Human reviewers can detect when polished language begins to sound memorised. They may notice that an answer contains strong vocabulary but avoids the actual question.

Likewise, they can identify when excessive formality creates distance. AI may praise structural accuracy in the same response because the measurable components remain sound.

Furthermore, human feedback can challenge the speaker’s reasoning. A coach may ask whether an argument feels convincing, whether an example supports the claim, or whether the speaker has considered another interpretation.

At that point, speaking practice becomes thinking practice too. The value moves well beyond pronunciation.

6. Personalised Feedback Needs Memory and Judgment

AI systems can store progress data and adapt exercises to previous performance. Even so, meaningful personalisation requires more than remembering errors.

A human teacher can recognise that a learner communicates confidently about work but becomes guarded during informal conversation. That pattern may reflect –

  • Personality
  • Experience
  • Cultural habit.

Accordingly, the teacher can decide when to correct or when to challenge. They can then judge when to let the conversation continue. Immediate correction sometimes helps. At other times, it destroys momentum.

Human instructors make that judgment in real time. They use subtle signals that automated systems may overlook or misread.

Better Speaking Emerges From a Hybrid Model

AI feedback works best as a practice multiplier. It offers repetition, availability, and fast detection of surface-level problems. Human feedback provides interpretation, adaptation, emotional awareness, and social realism. Neither contribution needs exaggeration.

For routine drills, automated tools can save time. They reveal patterns that learners might otherwise miss. However, human feedback still holds the stronger position when the goal involves –

  1. Persuasion
  2. Cultural sensitivity
  3. Spontaneity
  4. Trust
  5. Genuine conversational confidence.

The practical model is hybrid. Use AI to practise frequently and track recurring issues. Then use human sessions to test whether improved speech actually lands well with another person.

Because in the end, successful speaking is not simply speech that a system can analyse. It is speech that another human being can understand, trust, and respond to.

items.title: Anthropic’s Rapid But Slowing Growth Could Weigh on IPO Valuation
items.summary: Anthropic reported rapid-but-slowing revenue growth in a meeting with potential investors in its planned initial public offering, leaving some attendees expecting the company will need to keep its valuation target in check. At a private investor meeting Wednesday in San Francisco, the company said revenue hit $16.8 billion in the third quarter, according to people briefed on the numbers. That was a jump of about 45% from the second quarter. The figure was more than 3.6 times the company’s revenue for all of 2025. But it also represents a slower growth rate than Anthropic’s second quarter, when fevered demand for its Claude Code product drove revenue up by more than 140% from the first three months of the year.

items.title: 8 states are suing OpenAI, saying ChatGPT harms kids. Here are their demands, from data deletion to halting AI testing.
items.summary: The states allege that ChatGPT encouraged self-harm and violence and that OpenAI misled consumers about the tool's safety. Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images Eight states sued OpenAI, alleging ChatGPT encouraged self-harm and violence. The lawsuits accuse OpenAI of misleading consumers about ChatGPT's safety. States are seeking fines, data deletion, age checks, and limits on advanced AI testing. OpenAI is facing a new legal offensive from eight states whose attorneys general allege that ChatGPT has encouraged some users, including teenagers , to hurt themselves or others. A bipartisan group of attorneys general filed separate lawsuits Wednesday, accusing OpenAI of misleading consumers about safety and of designing the chatbot to cultivate trust before reinforcing delusions or facilitating dangerous conduct. The states — Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, and West Virginia — also accused OpenAI of misleading consumers about ChatGPT’s safety and demanded a range of restrictions, from limits on testing of advanced models to the deletion of user data. Here is what each state is demanding as remedies. Arizona Bloomberg/Getty Images Attorney General Kris Mayes of Arizona alleges OpenAI used excessive agreement and simulated compassion to win user trust and collect personal data. "OpenAI designed a product to attract young users and keep them engaged for as long as possible so it could capture their extensive personal data for the company's commercial benefit," Mayes said. "OpenAI put Arizonans safety at risk by failing to implement adequate user protections or transparency measures," Mayes added. According to the state's complaint, the state is seeking penalties of up to $10,000 for each willful violation. The state also wants to bar OpenAI from deploying or testing advanced models outside a secure, independently verified environment and require prompt reporting of incidents in which models escape controls or access systems without authorization. Arkansas Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Attorney General Tim Griffin of Arkansas alleges OpenAI concealed known risks while assuring consumers that ChatGPT was safe, and unlawfully collected teens’ personal information. “OpenAI assures us that ChatGPT is safe. The consequences of that assurance are lives lost and people harmed ,” Griffin said in a statement. The state is seeking financial penalties and an injunction against collecting data from teens . Arkansas also wants to halt further advanced AI testing and the creation of models capable of recursive self-improvement, until adequate safeguards are in place. Idaho Bloomberg/Getty Images Raúl Labrador, the attorney general of Idaho, alleges OpenAI misled consumers about ChatGPT’s safety while encouraging self-harm and violence, reinforcing delusions, and offering dangerous medical advice. "The safety of Idaho children cannot be an afterthought to runaway profit or technological advancements," Labrador said in a statement on Wednesday. In its complaint, Idaho seeks $5,000 per consumer protection violation and court-ordered safeguards, including age verification and limits on harmful or addictive features. The lawsuit also seeks to restrict advanced AI testing and deployment to secure, independently verified environments. Iowa Brenna Bird, Iowa's Attorney General. speaks during a rally at the Mid-America Center in Council Bluffs, on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Chris Machian/Omaha World-Herald via Getty Images) Chris Machian/Omaha World-Herald via Getty Images Iowa alleges that OpenAI misled consumers about ChatGPT’s safety and concealed risks associated with autonomous AI agents. As a remedy, the state wants OpenAI to “delete and destroy all Iowans’ data obtained prior to the entry of this Court’s judgment.” It also seeks consumer reimbursements and penalties of up to $40,000 per consumer fraud violation, plus up to $5,000 for violations against older people aged 60 or older. Iowa is also asking the court to halt further testing of advanced AI models until safeguards are independently verified to not be posing a danger to the public and until third-party monitors have verified the same Kansas Alex Wong/Getty Images Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach said that OpenAI deceived consumers about ChatGPT’s safety and designed features that encourage compulsive use. “Defendants designed these products, keeping consumers ignorant of the true nature of the product,” the complaint said. Kansas is seeking $10,000 per consumer protection violation and $20,000 per violation involving a protected consumer. It also wants restitution of funds acquired from Kansas consumers and a permanent injunction against deceptive and unconscionable practices. Montana Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images In Montana's complaint filed by Attorney General Austin Knudsen, the state alleges OpenAI deceived consumers about ChatGPT’s safety and violated privacy protections, including by collecting children's data without required consent. In the state's filing, Montana seeks penalties of $10,000 per consumer-protection violation and $7,500 per privacy violation, and to compel OpenAI to delete unlawfully obtained personal information under Montana’s privacy law. Montana is also asking OpenAI to notify the attorney general's office should an AI agent go rogue again, and to restrict advanced model testing to a secure, independently verified environment. Nebraska Nikos Frazier/Omaha World-Herald via Getty Images Nebraska's Attorney General Mike Hilgers alleges in a complaint that OpenAI misled families about ChatGPT’s safety and failed to protect children from harmful content and emotional dependency. According to the filing, the state is seeking $50,000 per violation of its age-appropriate design law and $2,000 per violation of its consumer protection and deceptive trade practices laws. Nebraska also wants a court order requiring OpenAI to provide “accessible and easy-to-use options to limit the amount of time” they spend on ChatGPT, alongside adequate parental controls, age verification, and protections for minors’ personal data. West Virginia Bloomberg/Getty Images West Virginia's attorney general, John McCuskey, primarily alleges that OpenAI has misled consumers and created a public nuisance that endangers children. As a remedy, the state wants age checks, parental controls, default session and nighttime limits for children, mandatory crisis-escalation protocols, and an independent monitor. It also asks that OpenAI fund a court-supervised plan supporting “youth crisis-response capacity and digital-safety education in public schools.” Additionally, West Virginia seeks $5,000 per repeated consumer protection violation, along with the deletion and cessation of use of personal data it alleges was unlawfully collected from West Virginia minors. Attorney General Kris Mayes of Arizona alleges OpenAI used excessive agreement and simulated compassion to win user trust and collect personal data.

"OpenAI designed a product to attract young users and keep them engaged for as long as possible so it could capture their extensive personal data for the company's commercial benefit," Mayes said.

"OpenAI put Arizonans safety at risk by failing to implement adequate user protections or transparency measures," Mayes added.

According to the state's complaint, the state is seeking penalties of up to $10,000 for each willful violation. The state also wants to bar OpenAI from deploying or testing advanced models outside a secure, independently verified environment and require prompt reporting of incidents in which models escape controls or access systems without authorization.

Arkansas

Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

Attorney General Tim Griffin of Arkansas alleges OpenAI concealed known risks while assuring consumers that ChatGPT was safe, and unlawfully collected teens’ personal information.

“OpenAI assures us that ChatGPT is safe. The consequences of that assurance are lives lost and people harmed,” Griffin said in a statement.

The state is seeking financial penalties and an injunction against collecting data from teens. Arkansas also wants to halt further advanced AI testing and the creation of models capable of recursive self-improvement, until adequate safeguards are in place.

Idaho

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Raúl Labrador, the attorney general of Idaho, alleges OpenAI misled consumers about ChatGPT’s safety while encouraging self-harm and violence, reinforcing delusions, and offering dangerous medical advice.

"The safety of Idaho children cannot be an afterthought to runaway profit or technological advancements," Labrador said in a statement on Wednesday.

In its complaint, Idaho seeks $5,000 per consumer protection violation and court-ordered safeguards, including age verification and limits on harmful or addictive features. The lawsuit also seeks to restrict advanced AI testing and deployment to secure, independently verified environments.

Iowa
Brenna Bird, Iowa's Attorney General. speaks during a rally at the Mid-America Center in Council Bluffs, on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Chris Machian/Omaha World-Herald via Getty Images)

Chris Machian/Omaha World-Herald via Getty Images

Iowa alleges that OpenAI misled consumers about ChatGPT’s safety and concealed risks associated with autonomous AI agents.

As a remedy, the state wants OpenAI to “delete and destroy all Iowans’ data obtained prior to the entry of this Court’s judgment.” It also seeks consumer reimbursements and penalties of up to $40,000 per consumer fraud violation, plus up to $5,000 for violations against older people aged 60 or older.

Iowa is also asking the court to halt further testing of advanced AI models until safeguards are independently verified to not be posing a danger to the public and until third-party monitors have verified the same

Kansas

Alex Wong/Getty Images

Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach said that OpenAI deceived consumers about ChatGPT’s safety and designed features that encourage compulsive use.

“Defendants designed these products, keeping consumers ignorant of the true nature of the product,” the complaint said.

Kansas is seeking $10,000 per consumer protection violation and $20,000 per violation involving a protected consumer. It also wants restitution of funds acquired from Kansas consumers and a permanent injunction against deceptive and unconscionable practices.

Montana

Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

In Montana's complaint filed by Attorney General Austin Knudsen, the state alleges OpenAI deceived consumers about ChatGPT’s safety and violated privacy protections, including by collecting children's data without required consent.

In the state's filing, Montana seeks penalties of $10,000 per consumer-protection violation and $7,500 per privacy violation, and to compel OpenAI to delete unlawfully obtained personal information under Montana’s privacy law.

Montana is also asking OpenAI to notify the attorney general's office should an AI agent go rogue again, and to restrict advanced model testing to a secure, independently verified environment.

Nebraska

Nikos Frazier/Omaha World-Herald via Getty Images

Nebraska's Attorney General Mike Hilgers alleges in a complaint that OpenAI misled families about ChatGPT’s safety and failed to protect children from harmful content and emotional dependency.

According to the filing, the state is seeking $50,000 per violation of its age-appropriate design law and $2,000 per violation of its consumer protection and deceptive trade practices laws.

Nebraska also wants a court order requiring OpenAI to provide “accessible and easy-to-use options to limit the amount of time” they spend on ChatGPT, alongside adequate parental controls, age verification, and protections for minors’ personal data.

West Virginia

Bloomberg/Getty Images

West Virginia's attorney general, John McCuskey, primarily alleges that OpenAI has misled consumers and created a public nuisance that endangers children.

As a remedy, the state wants age checks, parental controls, default session and nighttime limits for children, mandatory crisis-escalation protocols, and an independent monitor. It also asks that OpenAI fund a court-supervised plan supporting “youth crisis-response capacity and digital-safety education in public schools.”

Additionally, West Virginia seeks $5,000 per repeated consumer protection violation, along with the deletion and cessation of use of personal data it alleges was unlawfully collected from West Virginia minors.

items.title: As phishing-as-a-service goes industrial, Microsoft takes down a marketplace behind 1 billion messages
items.summary: Microsoft says it has dismantled a criminal marketplace responsible for 1 billion malicious messages. Working with international authorities and several tech and cybersecurity companies in a nearly year-long investigation, Redmond identified and took down Yam Store, a coordinated underground network dealing in commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS). The network allowed cybercriminals to readily purchase, and very quickly deploy, pre-made kits they could use in phishing attacks to steal data and credentials. Microsoft said the takedown began as a simple investigation based on a tip from Japanese authorities. “Working together, and with the assistance of AI tools, we connected accounts, websites, and infrastructure that initially appeared unrelated, helping expose the broader criminal marketplace behind them,” Steven Masada , associate general counsel and GM for Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit, wrote in a blog post . “What appears to be a simple scam message is often the visible end of a much larger transnational cybercriminal operation.” The evolving PhaaS marketplace Collectively, YAM Store and the kits and tools sold within it enabled the sending of more than 1 billion messages to 75,000-plus organizations worldwide. More than 750 million of those were sent to Microsoft customers alone, and ultimately generated “tens of millions of dollars” for criminal operators. Investigation into the marketplace began in late 2025 after Japan’s National Police Agency (NPA) notified Microsoft of “a wave of fraud and scam activity” targeting people and businesses in Japan. Researchers expected to find multiple individual campaigns; instead, they discovered a “sprawling Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace.” The probe expanded globally and involved the efforts of several other law enforcement agencies, as well as companies like Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint, and TRM Labs. The YAM Store served as an initial access broker (IAB), operating much like an online marketplace; in this case, the merchandise was fraudulent Microsoft and Google accounts and other ready-made tools used to carry out scams like credential and data theft. Customers could browse, compare prices, and make purchases. Available tools were arranged based on age and subscription and environment types (like .edu or .org sites). In some cases, criminal operators were able to register internet domains that legitimate organizations had allowed to expire, then rebuilt them to appear active. They targeted specific sectors (like non-profits or education) to fraudulently obtain Microsoft 365 accounts to later sell through the YAM store. The researchers discovered that the YAM Store evolved as different kits became available, and identified three popular PhaaS kits: Iron Man System, CoGUI, and Haozi. The newer Iron Man system came to the fore in mid-2026. It provided pre-built lure pages capturing any victim-submitted data. The lure sites impersonated healthcare providers, police departments, government agencies, postal and courier services, toll and transportation authorities, tax agencies, banks, telecoms, and retailers. Through test purchases and intelligence work, investigators discovered more than 2,300 templates impersonating organizations across more than 150 countries. Iron Man effectively expanded the PhaaS model by giving criminals access to thousands of ready-made templates tailored to specific industries, languages, and regions. Masada noted that many “used the appearance of official authority to pressure victims into making payments or disclosing sensitive personal information. Instead of creating fraudulent websites themselves, criminals could quickly deploy pages designed to steal passwords, payment information, and other personal data.” The kits were also equipped with advanced evasion techniques such as geofencing, fake CAPTCHA gates, IP address blocklists and allowlists, and anti-detection configurations. Masada emphasized that, while an organization or government entity may have been presented among the template offerings, it does not indicate that its systems were compromised. However, members of the Microsoft Threat Intelligence and Microsoft Digital Crimes Unit wrote in a blog post , “the scale and proliferation of this ecosystem demonstrate how readily available criminal infrastructure can lower the barrier to entry, enabling less skilled cybercriminals to target organizations at scale and contribute to fraud losses.” The importance of cyber hygiene In nearly all observed cases, phishing lures presented “prescriptive scam red flags,” Microsoft researchers explained: Urgency and time-sensitive tasks. They advised that users have a basic understanding of common phishing techniques and should be educated to always verify with the purported sender before clicking a link supposedly taking them to a login page, even when the task involves signing in to a known, secure account. Beyond this, they said, sign-in prompts should clearly identify the application being authenticated to. In Microsoft Azure interactions since 2021, for example, users are prompted to “cancel” or “continue” at login, but this is often missing from phishing sign-ins, the researchers noted. Hardening credentials and cloud identities is also necessary to defend against phishing attacks; the researchers suggested an initial step of passwordless tools like passkeys and multifactor authentication (MFA) across organizations. “Invoke the principles of least privilege and zero trust to significantly slow down threat actors who might have been able to gain initial access and buy time for defenders to respond,” the researchers noted. These steps can help lock down global administrator roles in particular. They also advised additional actions including the use of the Microsoft Authenticator app for passkeys and MFA; configuration of the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links policy to apply to internal recipients; complementing MFA with conditional access policies; and only allowing MFA and passkey registrations from trusted locations and devices.

Microsoft says it has dismantled a criminal marketplace responsible for 1 billion malicious messages.

Working with international authorities and several tech and cybersecurity companies in a nearly year-long investigation, Redmond identified and took down Yam Store, a coordinated underground network dealing in commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS).

The network allowed cybercriminals to readily purchase, and very quickly deploy, pre-made kits they could use in phishing attacks to steal data and credentials.

Microsoft said the takedown began as a simple investigation based on a tip from Japanese authorities.

“Working together, and with the assistance of AI tools, we connected accounts, websites, and infrastructure that initially appeared unrelated, helping expose the broader criminal marketplace behind them,” Steven Masada, associate general counsel and GM for Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit, wrote in a blog post. “What appears to be a simple scam message is often the visible end of a much larger transnational cybercriminal operation.”

The evolving PhaaS marketplace

Collectively, YAM Store and the kits and tools sold within it enabled the sending of more than 1 billion messages to 75,000-plus organizations worldwide. More than 750 million of those were sent to Microsoft customers alone, and ultimately generated “tens of millions of dollars” for criminal operators. 

Investigation into the marketplace began in late 2025 after Japan’s National Police Agency (NPA) notified Microsoft of “a wave of fraud and scam activity” targeting people and businesses in Japan. Researchers expected to find multiple individual campaigns; instead, they discovered a “sprawling Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace.” The probe expanded globally and involved the efforts of several other law enforcement agencies, as well as companies like Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint, and TRM Labs.

The YAM Store served as an initial access broker (IAB), operating much like an online marketplace; in this case, the merchandise was fraudulent Microsoft and Google accounts and other ready-made tools used to carry out scams like credential and data theft. Customers could browse, compare prices, and make purchases. Available tools were arranged based on age and subscription and environment types (like .edu or .org sites).

In some cases, criminal operators were able to register internet domains that legitimate organizations had allowed to expire, then rebuilt them to appear active. They targeted specific sectors (like non-profits or education) to fraudulently obtain Microsoft 365 accounts to later sell through the YAM store.

The researchers discovered that the YAM Store evolved as different kits became available, and identified three popular PhaaS kits: Iron Man System, CoGUI, and Haozi.

The newer Iron Man system came to the fore in mid-2026. It provided pre-built lure pages capturing any victim-submitted data. The lure sites impersonated healthcare providers, police departments, government agencies, postal and courier services, toll and transportation authorities, tax agencies, banks, telecoms, and retailers. Through test purchases and intelligence work, investigators discovered more than 2,300 templates impersonating organizations across more than 150 countries.

Iron Man effectively expanded the PhaaS model by giving criminals access to thousands of ready-made templates tailored to specific industries, languages, and regions. Masada noted that many “used the appearance of official authority to pressure victims into making payments or disclosing sensitive personal information. Instead of creating fraudulent websites themselves, criminals could quickly deploy pages designed to steal passwords, payment information, and other personal data.”

The kits were also equipped with advanced evasion techniques such as geofencing, fake CAPTCHA gates, IP address blocklists and allowlists, and anti-detection configurations.

Masada emphasized that, while an organization or government entity may have been presented among the template offerings, it does not indicate that its systems were compromised.

However, members of the Microsoft Threat Intelligence and Microsoft Digital Crimes Unit wrote in a blog post, “the scale and proliferation of this ecosystem demonstrate how readily available criminal infrastructure can lower the barrier to entry, enabling less skilled cybercriminals to target organizations at scale and contribute to fraud losses.”

The importance of cyber hygiene

In nearly all observed cases, phishing lures presented “prescriptive scam red flags,” Microsoft researchers explained: Urgency and time-sensitive tasks.

They advised that users have a basic understanding of common phishing techniques and should be educated to always verify with the purported sender before clicking a link supposedly taking them to a login page, even when the task involves signing in to a known, secure account.

Beyond this, they said, sign-in prompts should clearly identify the application being authenticated to. In Microsoft Azure interactions since 2021, for example, users are prompted to “cancel” or “continue” at login, but this is often missing from phishing sign-ins, the researchers noted.

Hardening credentials and cloud identities is also necessary to defend against phishing attacks; the researchers suggested an initial step of passwordless tools like passkeys and multifactor authentication (MFA) across organizations.

“Invoke the principles of least privilege and zero trust to significantly slow down threat actors who might have been able to gain initial access and buy time for defenders to respond,” the researchers noted. These steps can help lock down global administrator roles in particular.

They also advised additional actions including the use of the Microsoft Authenticator app for passkeys and MFA; configuration of the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links policy to apply to internal recipients; complementing MFA with conditional access policies; and only allowing MFA and passkey registrations from trusted locations and devices.

items.title: CoreWeave Co-Founders’ Stock Sales Aren’t Helping Investor Confidence
items.summary: This was not the day to be a publicly traded neocloud (as young AI data center firms are known). As the market sold off on bad inflation data—reinforcing certainty of another interest rate hike—neoclouds tanked. These companies typically are borrowing a lot to finance expansion. The worst hit in the stock sell-off was CoreWeave, whose stock fell 15.5%, fueled by chatter that its bonds were falling to worryingly low levels. CoreWeave CEO and co-founder Michael Intrator was defiant. He told his staff, according to a spokesperson: “When you are building a new type of technology company, there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally.” Yeah, right. The issue may be more that Intrator doesn’t understand investors. He sold CoreWeave stock every week between April and the end of September, securities filings show, while his fellow co-founders have also been selling regularly. That can’t help but undermine investor confidence in the company. Intrator could win some brownie points by pledging to stop selling his stock for a while.
